title: Is Anything Too Hard for the Lord?
paragraphs:
Is Anything Too Hard for the Lord?
The Question That Changes Everything When Life Falls Apart
There are moments in life when God's promises feel almost offensive.
Not because they are wrong.
Because they seem impossible.
The doctor lowers his eyes before speaking.
The marriage papers are already signed.
The addiction has returned again.
The child you prayed for is still gone.
The debt keeps growing.
The grief keeps breathing.
And somewhere between disappointment and exhaustion, a question begins whispering inside the soul:
"Has God finally reached a limit?"
That question is not new.
Thousands of years ago, an elderly woman stood in the same tension between divine promise and human impossibility.
Her name was Sarah.
She laughed when God spoke.
Not because she was joyful.
Because she was tired.
Tired people often laugh at miracles.
Genesis 18 records one of the most profound questions ever spoken by God Himself. The Hebrew text says:

"הֲיִפָּלֵא מֵיְהוָה דָּבָר"
(Ha-yippalē me-YHWH dābār?)
Most English translations render it:
"Is anything too hard for the LORD?" (Genesis 18:14)
But the Hebrew is even deeper.
The word "yippalē" comes from the root פלא (pala), meaning "wonderful," "extraordinary," "beyond human ability," "too marvelous to comprehend."
God was not merely asking whether something was difficult.
He was asking:

"Is anything beyond My power?"
"Is anything too extraordinary for Me?"
"Is anything outside the realm of what I can accomplish?"
Sarah was around ninety years old.
Abraham was about one hundred.
Biologically speaking, the promise was absurd.
Humanly speaking, the situation was finished.
But God has never required favorable circumstances to fulfill His word.
The miracle was never dependent on Sarah's ability.
It was dependent on God's faithfulness.
And that changes everything.
Because most of us secretly believe God works best when we can help Him.
We trust Him with what remains possible.
We trust ourselves with what seems impossible.
We pray while simultaneously calculating backup plans.
We worship while secretly preparing for disappointment.
We quote promises while emotionally expecting failure.
Yet throughout Scripture, God repeatedly chooses situations that cannot be explained apart from Him.
The Red Sea was impossible.
Jericho was impossible.
The giant was impossible.
The virgin birth was impossible.
The resurrection was impossible.
And perhaps that is precisely the point.
God's glory shines brightest where human ability ends.
When the angel Gabriel announced Christ's coming, he spoke words that intentionally echoed Genesis 18.
In Greek, Luke 1:37 reads:
"οὐκ ἀδυνατήσει παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ πᾶν ῥῆμα"
(ouk adynatēsei para tou Theou pan rhēma)
"For nothing will be impossible with God."
The Greek word "adynatēsei" means powerless, unable, incapable.
Gabriel was declaring:
"No word from God lacks the power to accomplish what it promises."
The God who opened Sarah's womb was preparing to enter history through Mary's womb.
The God who fulfilled an impossible promise in Genesis was preparing the greatest miracle in human history through Jesus Christ.
This is why Genesis 18 ultimately points beyond Isaac.
It points to Christ.
Because Isaac's birth was miraculous.
Jesus' birth was supernatural.
Isaac's birth overcame age.
Jesus' birth overcame nature itself.
Isaac brought joy to a family.
Jesus brought salvation to the world.
Every impossible promise in Scripture ultimately finds its fulfillment in Christ.
And nowhere do we see this more clearly than at the cross.
The cross looked like failure.
Public humiliation.
Political execution.
Religious scandal.
A dead Messiah hanging between criminals.
Everything appeared lost.
The disciples scattered.
Hope collapsed.
Faith shattered.
Darkness covered the land.
If anyone had walked past Golgotha that Friday afternoon, they would have concluded the story was over.
But God specializes in rewriting endings.
What looked like defeat became victory.
What looked like shame became redemption.
What looked like death became life.
What looked like a scandal became grace.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
And it is why the question from Genesis still matters today.
Because many people reading this have areas of life that feel buried behind stones too heavy to move.
Relationships beyond repair.
Dreams beyond recovery.
Wounds beyond healing.
Failures beyond forgiveness.
But Christianity does not stand upon positive thinking.
It stands upon an empty tomb.
The resurrection is God's eternal declaration that impossibility is never the final chapter for those who trust Him.
When Jesus stood before Lazarus' tomb, Martha expressed what many believers feel:
"Lord, if You had been here..."
In other words:
"God, You are late."
"God, You missed the window."
"God, the damage is already done."
"God, the story is over."
But Jesus walked to the grave anyway.
Because He was not merely entering a funeral.
He was entering a situation designed to reveal His glory.
And perhaps that is where some of us are today.
Not abandoned.
Not forgotten.
Not rejected.
Simply standing in a chapter where God has not yet finished writing.
The enemy wants you to judge God by your circumstances.
Scripture calls you to judge your circumstances by God.
The same Lord who asked Sarah, "Is anything too hard for the LORD?" remains unchanged.
His character has not weakened.
His power has not diminished.
His promises have not expired.
His mercy has not run dry.
His grace has not reached its limit.
The Hebrew Scriptures, the Greek New Testament, and the entire story of redemption converge on one breathtaking reality:
Nothing is too hard for the Lord because Jesus Christ has already conquered the hardest thing of all.
Sin.
Death.
Hell.
Judgment.
The greatest impossibility humanity ever faced was reconciliation with a holy God.
And Christ accomplished it through His death and resurrection.
If He can save sinners, He can sustain saints.
If He can conquer death, He can handle your situation.
If He can transform persecutors into apostles, prostitutes into worshipers, thieves into heirs of paradise, and broken failures into vessels of grace, then your story is not beyond His reach.
Maybe that is why this question refuses to disappear.
Because every generation eventually arrives at a place where human strength fails.
Every heart eventually encounters a circumstance too large to carry.
And in that moment, Genesis 18:14 echoes across centuries:
"Is anything too hard for the LORD?"
The answer remains exactly what it was when Abraham first heard it.
No.
Nothing.
Not your past.
Not your addiction.
Not your fear.
Not your shame.
Not your failure.
Not your grief.
Not your impossible situation.
Not even your hardest heart.
Jesus Christ is still rewriting stories.
He is still redeeming failures.
He is still restoring prodigals.
He is still healing wounds.
He is still calling sinners home.
He is still turning scandals into testimonies.
And perhaps the greatest miracle waiting to happen is not around you.
It is within you.
If this message spoke to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Because every share spreads the Gospel.
Every comment strengthens community.
Every testimony points someone closer to Christ.
And every redeemed life becomes proof that God's grace still writes better endings than sin ever could.
The same God who opened Sarah's womb, raised Lazarus from the grave, and raised Jesus from the dead is still writing stories today.
Maybe yours is next.
The chapter you're crying through today may become the testimony that glorifies God tomorrow.
